title: A man up a tree
hookLine: a man hangs from a branch by his teeth; someone asks why Bodhidharma came west (Gateless Gate 5)

lines: SPEAK AND FALL. STAY SILENT AND FAIL.
cards: A man is up a tree, hanging from a branch by his teeth. His hands grip nothing. His feet touch nothing.
Below him, a long drop. And someone under the tree calls up a question: why did Bodhidharma come from the west? It's a question Zen stories use to ask what this whole tradition is about.

If the man keeps quiet, he fails the person asking. If he opens his mouth to answer, he falls. That's the whole story, case five of the Gateless Gate, and it ends with a question for you: what would you do?

teach.h: XIANGYAN SETS IT UP AND STOPS.
teach.b: Back in year one, a koan was a short story or question meant to stop the thinking mind. Here is one at full squeeze. First, who tells it: a teacher named Xiangyan, Kyogen in Japanese.
He sets up the scene and stops. He never says what the man did; the koan hands the problem to whoever is listening. Second, the trap.
Answer, and you fall. Don't, and you've turned away someone who asked the biggest thing they could ask. The mind hunts for a third door: shout, nod, hum through your teeth.
A clever escape misses the point. This isn't a riddle with a trick answer. It's built to leave thinking with nowhere to stand.
Third, why a tree. This week's koans each carry some version of this pressure, and here there are no free hands and no ground.
That's a picture of a moment any life can bring: a hospital hallway, a phone call, a choice where every road costs something.
Zen students don't solve the case like a puzzle.
They stay with the squeeze long enough to find out who is hanging there. Fourth, the comment.
The compiler, Wumen, added a comment and a verse to each case. In paraphrase, he says even a flood of eloquence is no use here, and if you can answer in this spot, you bring dead things back to life.
He doesn't hand over the answer either. Some readers notice the man is still alive at the end.
The whole koan happens in one held breath, the teeth still holding.

how: In Rinzai Zen, students are given koans such as this one to hold through sitting and daily life, and they present their response to the teacher in private interview rather than writing an answer down.

games.q: what does “a man up a tree” mean?
o: a koan where every choice costs and no answer is given
a parable about the dangers of climbing too high
a Zen riddle with one clever trick answer to find

games.q: a man up a tree: tap the pairs.
p: the teacher who tells the case
the compiler who adds a comment
and you fail the one who asks

s: the koan ends by telling us what the man did
Xiangyan sets up the scene and stops; the question is left for the listener.
the man hangs by his teeth, hands and feet free of the tree
his hands grip no branch and his feet rest on nothing.
Wumen's comment says a clever enough speech will get you out
in paraphrase, he says even a flood of eloquence is no use here.

games.q: you're hanging from the branch by your teeth. someone below asks why Bodhidharma came from the west. what do you do?
games.why: Xiangyan never says. the case ends with the question, and Zen students take it into sitting and into the teacher's room.

practice: Bring to mind one choice in your life where every option seems to cost something, and don't solve it or list pros and cons.
Just hold it, the way the man holds the branch, and feel where the squeeze sits: the jaw, the chest, the hands. When the mind races for a third door, notice the racing and come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: A man up a tree. Xiangyan's koan, case five of the Gateless Gate: hanging by the teeth, asked the great question, with no safe way to speak or stay silent. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese title of Gateless Gate case 5, 'Xiangyan up a tree'. Pronunciation approximates Mandarin.

carryVoice: Your line: hanging by the teeth. Nothing has fallen yet, and the question is still yours. See you tomorrow.
